result.summary: Pausanias continues his catalogue of Olympic victor statues. He tells of Astylus of Croton, whose house became a prison, and of runners such as Chionis, Polites and Leonidas. He also notes boxers, pancratiasts, and a mare named Aura whose race ended in victory without a rider.

scenes.title: Astylus and Chionis statues
scenes.summary: Astylus is punished by Croton for running as a Syracusan. Pausanias then corrects those who think Chionis set up his own pillar and statue.
scenes.stakes: Astylus loses his statue and house at home after switching his allegiance to please Hiero.

scenes.title: Famous Olympic runners
scenes.summary: Hermogenes, Polites and Leonidas are praised for their running victories.

scenes.title: Boxers, pancratiasts and sculptors
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists statues of Scaeus, Diallus, Thersilochus, Aristion, Bycelus, Mnaseas, Agemachus and Tisander, with their sculptors.

scenes.title: Horses and further victors
scenes.summary: The mare Aura wins after losing her rider, and the sons of Phidolas honour the horse Lycus. Other statues of Agathinus, Telemachus and Aristophon are noted.

analysis.text: Statues at Olympia record civic pride and rivalry, and Pausanias uses them to show how cities honoured or punished athletes.
Athletes switching city allegiance for a tyrant's favour, as Astylus did, shows how politics intruded on Greek games.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes that Corinth and Argos kept no early victor lists for their games, unlike Elis for Olympia.

language_notes.text: The stade was the single-length footrace (about 190 metres); the double course (diaulos) was one length there and back.
Hiero, son of Dinomenes, was the tyrant of Syracuse. Astylus's switch of allegiance to flatter him was treated as betrayal by Croton.
The race in heavy armour (hoplite race) was added to the Olympic programme later; Pausanias argues Chionis could not have anticipated it, so the pillar's list proves nothing about authorship.
The wild olive crown was the Olympic prize, cut from a sacred tree at Olympia.
Pausanias describes a second-day contest among four runners chosen by lot, apparently the winners of earlier races, a rule that is obscure to modern readers.
The inscription links the victory to the Samians' exile from their island; they later returned, and the statue was set up then.
The pancratium was a brutal combined contest of wrestling and boxing, with few rules.
'The tyrant' refers to a statue mentioned just before this passage, presumably of a tyrant whom Pausanias has described.
A hoplite here means a runner in the race in armour, the hoplite race.
Pausanias means that no victor lists survived for these games, so he cannot check Tisander's wins there.
Aura means 'breeze' in Greek, a fitting name for a swift mare.

context_notes.text: Lacinian Hera was worshipped at a famous sanctuary near Croton in southern Italy. Removing the statue was a formal public disgrace.
Myro was a renowned Athenian bronze sculptor of the fifth century BC, best known for his Discus Thrower.
Ceramus was a city in Caria, in southwestern Asia Minor.
Polycletus of Argos was one of the most famous Greek sculptors of the fifth century BC.
Naxos in Sicily was an early Greek colony, said to be founded from Chalcis; it was later destroyed by Dionysius of Syracuse.
The Pythian games were held at Delphi in honour of Apollo, and ranked just below Olympia.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias sharply calls the mistaken 'simple', using mild scorn to correct earlier opinion and assert his authority as a careful observer.
The question exposes the flaw in the opposing view by logic rather than assertion, as no one could list a race not yet created.
The nickname 'Horse' vividly conveys Hermogenes's speed and endurance in a single word.
The mare is given human awareness and purpose, finishing the course, hearing the trumpet and knowing she had won.
Pausanias steps back with a dry, skeptical aside, leaving the discrepancy for readers instead of resolving it.
